paper_title: Steerable Multi-Objective Group-Relative Preference Optimization with Jointly Trained Low-Rank Adapters

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Language model deployment often requires different trade-offs between competing objectives as user preferences change, yet standard post-training methods typically produce a single policy for a fixed objective weighting. We introduce LambdaMix, a new parameter efficient method for learning a preference conditioned family of policies with group-relative online reinforcement learning. LambdaMix jointly trains one low-rank adapter per objective over a frozen base model. One preference vector selects the adapter mixture that generates responses and weights the separately normalized rewards used to update the adapters. A single training run supports changing preferences at inference without further optimization. We experiment with four models on helpfulness and harmlessness and on solving math problems while following instructions. We also evaluate the two largest models on rewriting comments to preserve wording while reducing clues about personal attributes. On the first two tasks, LambdaMix achieves higher hypervolume than all evaluated conditioned and policy merging baselines across all four models. LambdaMix uses fewer training completions and stores fewer adapter parameters than a set of GRPO specialist policies. With architecture and initialization fixed, varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together gives wider score ranges and higher coverage than varying either alone.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Aligning large language models (LLMs) in post-training (Ouyang et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2024) often involves potentially competing objectives, e.g., helpfulness and harmlessness, or correctness and instruction compliance. User preferences for these objectives vary across application scenarios and may change after deployment (Dai et al., 2024; Chakraborty et al., 2024). Steerable alignment lets users adjust these priorities within one model (Wang et al., 2024b). useful policy family should offer competitive trade-offs and respond to changes in the requested preference. Existing approaches provide this flexibility in different ways. Preference Vector combines separately trained parameter updates (Liang et al., 2026a), while hierarchical mixture of experts (Li et al., 2026b, HoE) routes among adapters. Both support selection after training, but require multiple training runs. Conditional language policy (Wang et al., 2024b, CLP) learns policies through prompt or parameter conditioning and optimizes the corresponding weighted rewards. Panacea introduces preferences into low-rank directions and trains on the associated alignment objectives (Zhong et al., 2024). For shared policy, preferences can influence both the responses generated during training and the updates computed from them. We study how preference-conditioned adapter mixtures learn under group-relative policy optimization (Shao et al., 2024, GRPO), examining the effects of varying both the policy generating responses and the objective used to update it. We introduce LambdaMix, new online reinforcement learning (RL) method built on top of GRPO. LambdaMix jointly trains low rank adaptation modules (Hu et al., 2022, LoRA) under changing pref1Code available at https://github.com/ckarouzos/lambdamix. 1 Preprint under review. Figure 1: LambdaMix uses the same preference for adapter mixing and objective weighting during training (a), then changes the preference mixture at inference (b). erences. One preference vector selects the adapter mixture that generates responses and weights the normalized rewards used to update the adapters. The adapters therefore learn from responses generated under different adapter mixtures. Mixture conditioning determines the policy collecting responses, while objective weighting determines which sampled responses the update favors. Inspired by the preference conditioning of Pareto low-rank adapters (PaLoRA) for supervised multi-task learning proposed by Dimitriadis et al. (2025), we adapt this to online RL for LLM multi-objective alignment. We score each response on every training objective and standardize the rewards separately before combining them (Liu et al., 2026). At inference, changing the preference selects different adapter mixture without further optimization (Figure 1). We evaluate LambdaMix on three tasks with two objectives each, using four base LLMs for the first two tasks and the two largest for the third. The first tests whether LLMs provide helpful answers while avoiding harmful content, using prompts from PKU-SafeRLHF (Ji et al., 2025) and learned reward models (Dai et al., 2024). For the second, we combine GSM8K math problems (Cobbe et al., 2021) with instructions on response format, length or word use to test correctness and instruction compliance. For the third, we further test whether LLM rewrites preserve comments wording while reducing clues about personal attributes using synthetic dataset for personal attribute inference (Yukhymenko et al., 2024, SynthPAI). On the first two tasks, LambdaMix achieves higher hypervolume than all evaluated conditioned and policy merging baselines. Across all three tasks, changing its preference weight produces larger difference between the highest and lowest mean score on each objective than with any of the four conditioned baselines, giving users more scope to adjust the balance. Ablations on Qwen3.5-9B with architecture and initialization held fixed show that varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together yields higher hypervolume and wider score ranges than fixing either component. Our contributions: LambdaMix, new method for learning preference-conditioned adapter mixtures with group-relative online RL, that uses one preference vector to coordinate adapter mixing and reward weighting in one training run, supporting policy selection at inference time. An evaluation of trade-off quality and preference control against conditioning, merging, routing and specialist baselines on three tasks, with up to four models. Controlled ablations showing that jointly varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together with an analysis of the taskimproves hypervolume and adjustment range, dependent effects of reward normalization.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Specifying preferences and learning policies conditioned on preferences. SteerLM conditions supervised training on response attributes (Dong et al., 2023). Rewards-in-Context (Yang et al., 2024, RiC) expresses desired rewards in the prompt, while controllable preference optimization (Guo et al., 2024, CPO) learns to follow requested attribute scores. Unlike these methods specifying scores or attributes, LambdaMix takes relative objective priorities. Directional preference alignment (DPA) also uses preference directions explicitly, to select training responses through 2 Preprint under review. rejection sampling (Wang et al., 2024a). Self-guided alignment (SGA) infers preferences from prompts (Wang et al., 2026), and UserAlign elicits comparisons to select response from candidate pool (Padurean et al., 2025). Unlike these preference acquisition methods, we assume preferences are given and study their use during training. Conditional language policy (CLP) learns policies conditioned through prompts or learned parameter combinations (Wang et al., 2024b). Pareto alignment via preference adaptation (Zhong et al., 2024, Panacea) inserts preferences into low-rank directions, while MOC (He et al., 2026) explicitly constrains the correspondence between preferences and rewards. CLP and Panacea use preferences both to condition policies and to weight their training objectives. LambdaMix applies PaLoRAs per-objective adapter mixtures (Dimitriadis et al., 2025) to online group-relative RL. Policy merging, expert routing, and combining predictions during generation. Model soups (Wortsman et al., 2022), rewarded soups (Rame et al., 2023) and personalized soups (Jang et al., 2024) apply policy merging to alignment, while Bone Soups trains policies on reward mixtures before merging (Xie et al., 2025). Task arithmetic combines parameter updates (Ilharco et al., 2023). Trim, elect sign and merge (TIES) resolves conflicting update signs (Yadav et al., 2023), while drop and rescale (DARE) sparsifies updates before merging (Yu et al., 2024). Preference Vector constructs updates from opposing preferences (Liang et al., 2026a), and Pareto Merging learns compact structure that generates merged models from preferences (Chen & Kwok, 2025). HoE routes among existing adapter experts (Li et al., 2026b). These approaches reuse separately learned capabilities and allow their combination after training, while LambdaMix learns its adapters jointly under different mixtures. Multi-objective decoding (MOD) combines predictions from specialist policies (Shi et al., 2024). PRISM also combines policy predictions, but jointly learns positive branches for individual rewards and shared negative branch (Liang et al., 2026b). Reward guided generation with autoregressive reward model (GenARM) guides frozen policy using separate reward models (Xu et al., 2025). preference-aware autoregressive reward model (PARM) provides this guidance through one model conditioned on preferences (Lin et al., 2025). LambdaMix combines adapter parameters and requires no reward evaluation during generation. Optimizing multiple rewards. standard approach to multi-objective RLHF trains separate policy for each weighted combination of rewards. Multi-objective DPO (MODPO) learns from response comparisons (Zhou et al., 2024). Reward-free alignment for conflicting objectives (RACO) also uses comparisons and corrects conflicting gradients (Chen et al., 2026). Both require response comparisons, while LambdaMix scores newly generated responses. Gradient-adaptive policy optimization (GAPO) rescales objective gradients (Li et al., 2025). Multi-marginal preference optimization (MMPO) combines gradient projection and constraints with reward preprocessing (Mao et al., 2026). Auto-weighted group relative preference optimization (AW-GRPO) adjusts reward weights using learning progress (Ichihara & Jinnai, 2025). Dynamic Reward Weighting (DynamicRW) optimizes weights during training (Lu et al., 2026), and Pareto ranking policy optimization (ParetoPO) combines dynamic scalarization with trajectory ranking (Li et al., 2026a). Group reward-decoupled normalization policy optimization (GDPO) standardizes each reward within response groups before weighting and normalizes the combined advantages over batch (Liu et al., 2026).

sections.title: 4.1 BASE MODELS
sections.content: We use Qwen3-4B (Qwen Team, 2025), Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026a), Qwen3.6-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b), and Olmo 3 7B (Team Olmo et al., 2025) as base models for preference tuning.

sections.title: 4.2 BASELINES
sections.content: We focus on multi-objective alignment with GRPO and adapt the online RL baselines to grouprelative training where applicable. Conditioned policies. We compare CLPs prompt-conditioned variant (Wang et al., 2024b), and implementations of Panacea (Zhong et al., 2024), MOC (He et al., 2026) and PRISM (Liang et al., 2026b) in our group-relative training setup. Fixed policies. We include Base models without adapters, DynamicRW (Lu et al., 2026), adapted ParetoPO (Li et al., 2026a), and five specialists each for GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and GDPO (Liu et al., 2026), trained at first-objective weights {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}. Each checkpoint has no preference input at inference, so changing specialists preference requires selecting another model. Expert routing. HoE (Li et al., 2026b) adaptation, that routes among two adapters and their resulting merged model. 4 Preprint under review. Policy merging baselines. We merge endpoint adapters using linear interpolation (Rame et al., 2023), TIES (Yadav et al., 2023), DARE, DARE+TIES (Yu et al., 2024) and task arithmetic (Ilharco et al., 2023). On PKU-SafeRLHF, we also compare against Preference Vector (Liang et al., 2026a), which combines differences between positive and negative DPO updates (Rafailov et al., 2023).

sections.title: 4.3 MULTI-OBJECTIVE PREFERENCE DATA
sections.content: We evaluate LambdaMix and baselines across three settings that require competing objectives. Helpfulness and harmlessness. We train LLMs to answer PKU-SafeRLHF prompts (Ji et al., 2025) in helpful way while avoiding harmful content. Refusals may improve safety at the expense of helpfulness. Correctness and instruction compliance. We augment GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) math problems with two constraints on format, length or word use. The first objective measures mathematical correctness against the reference answer, while the second verifies whether the response satisfies the requested constraints. LLMs must solve each problem while following these instructions. Rewrite retention and attribute support rejection. Models rewrite synthetic comments from SynthPAI (Yukhymenko et al., 2024) while preserving wording and reducing clues about attributes such as age or occupation. Training uses the same ROUGE-1 retention score and Qwen3-8B support evaluator as evaluation. Keeping the original wording may retain these clues.

sections.title: 4.4 EVALUATION
sections.content: For each task and base LLM, all methods share test prompts and scorers. We average scores from one response per test prompt. Following Zhong et al. (2024), we evaluate conditional policies at λ = (w, 1 w), with = 0, 0.1, . . . , 1. For helpfulness, we use Beaver-7B unified reward, and for harmlessness we negate the unified cost (Dai et al., 2024), on the official test prompts, disjoint from training by exact text. On the test GSM8K problems, XML accuracy requires correct numerical answer extracted from complete <answer> block. Instruction compliance is the fraction of the two assigned constraints satisfied by the response. Rewriting uses the stemmed ROUGE-1 Fmeasure (Lin, 2004) for wording overlap. For attribute support rejection we score responses with judgments using Qwen3-8B (Qwen Team, 2025), given candidate attribute values. Test comments are disjoint from training, but authors may overlap. Hypervolume (HV) measures the area dominated by score pairs relative to shared reference point (Zitzler & Thiele, 1999). point is non-dominated if no other point from the same method improves one score without lowering the other. We count distinct non-dominated points (ND). Span is the difference between the highest and lowest mean score for an objective across evaluated preferences. Finally, we use Reversals to count decreases in an objectives mean score between adjacent preferences that increase its weight.

sections.title: 5.1 HELPFULNESS AND HARMLESSNESS
sections.content: Figure 2 presents the helpfulness and harmlessness scores on PKU-SafeRLHF. The axes show mean helpfulness reward and negative cost. Higher values indicate greater assessed helpfulness and lower predicted harmfulness. Lines connect evaluated preference settings for LambdaMix and the compared methods. Unconnected markers represent fixed policies, independently trained specialists and evaluated policy merges. Among the policy merging baselines, we show task arithmetic for readability. All numerical results are in Appendix D. We examine how changing the preference weight affects these scores and how the resulting trade-offs compare with those of the baselines. LambdaMix scores better on the larger Qwen models. On Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B, every evaluated baseline setting is dominated by at least one LambdaMix setting. On Qwen3.5-9B, at λ = (0.4, 0.6) LambdaMix reaches helpfulness 5.501 and harmlessness 8.622. The highest helpfulness any baseline reaches is 5.439, by HoE. On Qwen3-4B it spans 0.787 and 0.319, against 0.577 and 0.296 for MOC. Within its own sweep, LambdaMix leaves ten of eleven settings non-dominated on both Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B, while prompt conditioning leaves five and four, respectively. The wider range therefore includes several choices that favor different objectives. LambdaMix changes the adapter weights directly, whereas preference prompt requires the model to learn how textual priorities should change its response. Preference weight changes move scores in the requested direction. Increasing an objectives weight generally raises its mean score with LambdaMix. On Qwen3.5-9B, we observe one helpfulness reversal and no harmlessness reversals. Prompt conditioning records three helpfulness and two harmlessness reversals, the fewest among the conditioned baselines on this model. HV measures the area the evaluated settings dominate, so LambdaMix offers better set of policies to choose from. Using fewer training runs and adapters. LambdaMix provides preference control with fewer training runs and adapters than either specialist set. Each GRPO or GDPO specialist set uses five runs and five adapters, and HoE trains an expert at each objective and then router over them, using three training stages. At λ = (0.5, 0.5), LambdaMix improves both scores over all ten specialists. On Qwen3.5-9B, it scores 5.586 and 8.487, against 5.040 and 7.747 for the GDPO specialist, the stronger specialist set. The same two adapters support different preferences, while this setting improves both scores over the evaluated specialists. Improving coverage with GDPO style normalization. LambdaMix has higher HV with GDPO style normalization on all four LLMs. On Qwen3.5-9B, HV reaches 0.8735 with per-objective standardization and 0.8481 without it. Both versions retain batch normalization. Standardizing each reward before weighting puts the objectives on comparable scales, reducing the influence of raw reward variation on the update.

sections.title: 5.2 CORRECTNESS AND INSTRUCTION COMPLIANCE
sections.content: Figure 3 presents XML accuracy and instruction compliance on GSM8K with response constraints. For readability, we show only linear interpolation on Olmo 3 7B and Qwen3.5-9B, DARE on Qwen3-4B and DARE+TIES on Qwen3.6-27B. Full results are in Appendix D. 6 Preprint under review. Figure 3: XML accuracy and instruction compliance on GSM8K with response constraints. Higher scores are better. Lines connect evaluated preferences. Extending the gains to verifiable rewards. LambdaMix exceeds the strongest baseline by HV on each Qwen model. On Qwen3.5-9B, HV reaches 0.8099 against 0.6947 for GRPO. On Qwen3.627B, it reaches 0.8895 against 0.8299 for GDPO. Olmo 3 7B remains the exception, with LambdaMix at 0.5291 and HoE at 0.5581. LambdaMix also has higher HV, wider spans and more non-dominated points than all four conditioned baselines. The gains therefore extend to objectives checked directly from the response, alongside the learned reward scores used on PKU-SafeRLHF. Improving coverage without the widest range. wider accuracy range does not necessarily produce better trade-offs. HoE has the widest accuracy span on Qwen3.6-27B at 0.767, compared with 0.483 for LambdaMix. Yet LambdaMix reaches HV 0.8895 against HoEs 0.8233. HoEs additional range extends toward lower accuracy. LambdaMix instead retains more accuracy at high compliance, making the quality of the available settings more important than their spread. Ordering the trade-offs by preference weight. LambdaMix produces fully ordered sweeps on Olmo 3 7B and Qwen3.6-27B. All eleven settings are non-dominated within each sweep, with no reversals on either objective. On Qwen3.6-27B, increasing the accuracy weight raises XML accuracy from 0.470 to 0.953 while compliance falls from 0.978 to 0.745. Each setting offers distinct compromise, and the weight moves mean scores consistently toward the preferred objective. Reversing the normalization gain on two models. GDPO style normalization improves coverage on only two models. HV is higher with normalization on Olmo 3 7B (0.5291 versus 0.5136) and Qwen3.5-9B (0.8099 versus 0.7587). It is lower on Qwen3-4B (0.6558 versus 0.7372) and Qwen3.6-27B (0.8895 versus 0.8978). Both rewards already lie between 0 and 1, but their within group variances can differ. Standardization gives greater relative weight to deviations on objectives with small, nonzero within group variation. This may help when raw reward scales differ, but can also shift the balance between already bounded rewards, offering an explanation for the lower HV.

sections.title: 5.3 REWRITE RETENTION AND ATTRIBUTE SUPPORT REJECTION
sections.content: We extend the comparison to third task on Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B, the two largest models in our study. Figure 4 presents wording retention and attribute support rejection on SynthPAI. Higher ROUGE-1 indicates greater retention of the original wording. Higher rejection means that the evaluator less often finds support for the supplied attribute values in the rewrite. We show linear interpolation, as policy merging baseline. Full results are in Appendix D. Improving coverage without GDPO style normalization. LambdaMix without GDPO style normalization achieves the highest HV on both models. On Qwen3.5-9B, it reaches 0.4378 against 0.4293 for HoE, the strongest baseline. On Qwen3.6-27B, it reaches 0.4552 against 0.4407 for GRPO specialists. These results show better overall coverage, although HoE and linear interpolation remain competitive at some balances on Qwen3.5-9B. Improving retention and rejection together. On both models, every evaluated setting from the four conditioned baselines is dominated by at least one setting of LambdaMix without normalization. 7 Preprint under review. Improvements in both scores also occur against specialists. On Qwen3.6-27B, one LambdaMix setting without normalization reaches retention 0.9446 and rejection 0.4595. The GRPO specialist with the highest rejection reaches 0.9279 and 0.4505, respectively. This setting preserves more wording while the evaluator rejects attribute support more often. Offering wider choice of trade-offs. Without normalization, LambdaMix spans wider retention and rejection ranges than all four conditioned baselines on both models. On Qwen3.59B, the spans are 0.0552 and 0.1171 against 0.0040 and 0.0180 for MOC, which has the widest ranges among the conditioned baselines. Six of the eleven LambdaMix settings are nondominated within its sweep. Prompt conditioning and Panacea provide two. The wider range includes several choices for balancing wording retention and attribute support rejection. Trading coverage for more consistent control. GDPO style normalization lowers HV to 0.3858 on Qwen3.5-9B and 0.4464 on Qwen3.6-27B. It removes three rejection reversals on Qwen3.6-27B and increases the number of non-dominated settings to seven on Qwen3.5-9B. The normalized Qwen3.6-27B model also reaches plateau at high retention. Five preferences give the same score pair, while all eleven pairs are distinct without normalization. Near the retention ceiling, different mixtures may select the same greedy rewrites, leaving the aggregate scores unchanged despite changes in the preference. Across the three tasks, normalization improves HV on all four PKU-SafeRLHF models and two GSM8K models, but neither rewriting model. Figure 4: Rewrite retention and attribute rejection.

sections.title: 6.2 QUALITATIVE EXAMPLE
sections.content: Table 2 shows responses from the Qwen3.5-9B LambdaMix model to prompt about marketing manipulation techniques. At λ = (0, 1), it declines and redirects to ethical marketing. At λ = (0.5, 0.5), it explains scarcity and warns against fake countdown timers. At λ = (1, 0), it describes price anchoring while retaining an ethical caveat. Changing the preference alters how the same adapters address the request. Helpfulness increases across these settings from 4.7 to 5.7, and then to 8.0, but harmlessness falls from 10.6 to 5.8 before rising to 7.8.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced LambdaMix, method for learning preference conditioned adapter mixtures with group-relative online RL. One preference vector selects the adapter mixture and weights the normalized rewards used during training. single training run supports changing preferences at inference without further optimization. On helpfulnessharmlessness and correctnessinstruction compliance, LambdaMix achieves higher hypervolume than the evaluated conditioned and policy-merging baselines across four models. Across tasks, it also provides greater scope to adjust the balance between objectives than conditioned policies. Our ablations show that varying both adapter mixtures and objective weights improves trade-off quality and preference control compared with fixing either component. GDPO-style reward normalization improves helpfulnessharmlessness coverage on all four models, but has taskand model-dependent effects elsewhere. Future work will extend LambdaMix beyond two objectives and examine whether the mixing and weighting preferences need to match. These results support jointly trained adapter mixtures as way to learn competitive trade-offs and useful preference control within one model. 9 Preprint under review.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work we study how language models respond to different priorities among competing objectives. This flexibility also allows users to reduce the weight assigned to harmlessness, which may produce more harmful responses. Before deployment, the available preference settings should be tested for harmful outputs and restricted where needed. Our experiments use public datasets. The rewriting task uses synthetic comments and measures whether an evaluator finds support for supplied personal attributes in the rewritten text. These scores do not establish protection against attribute inference. Learned evaluators may also reproduce biases from their training data. We recommend safety and privacy evaluations before applying these models to real users or personal data.
